examples.prompt: A normal distribution has mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. Find $P(\mu - 2\sigma \le x \le \mu)$.
examples.title: Example A – Finding Area Between Two Values
steps: The interval from $\mu-2\sigma$ to $\mu$ is the left half of the $\mu\pm 2\sigma$ range.
The total area within $\mu\pm 2\sigma$ is 95%, so the area from $\mu-2\sigma$ to $\mu$ is half of that.
95% ÷ 2 = 47.5%, plus the 34% from $\mu-\sigma$ to $\mu$? Let's break it: 13.5% (from -2σ to -1σ) + 34% (from -1σ to μ) = 47.5%.
So $P(\mu-2\sigma \le x \le \mu) = 0.475$.

examples.prompt: Using the same test (μ=55, σ=12), an agency hires only applicants with scores of 67 or greater. What percent are eligible?
steps: 67 is μ + 1σ. The area to the right of μ + 1σ is half of the remaining 32% (100% - 68%) = 16%.
So about 16% of test-takers are eligible.

blocks.title: Normal Distributions and the Empirical Rule

confusionCorner.title: Don't Forget the Symmetry
confusionCorner.body: The empirical rule percentages are split equally on both sides of the mean. For example, the area from $\mu$ to $\mu+\sigma$ is 34%, not 68%. Always draw the curve and shade the region you need.

teacherCues: Draw a bell-shaped curve on the board. Mark the mean and the points μ±σ, μ±2σ, μ±3σ. Label the 68%, 95%, 99.7% areas.
Ask: 'If a data set is normally distributed, what percent of the data is above the mean?'

discoveryHook.scenario: From heights and test scores to the weights of cereal boxes, many real-world data sets follow a bell-shaped pattern called a normal distribution. Knowing just the mean and standard deviation, you can estimate the percentage of data within any range using the Empirical Rule!

explanation: A [[kw:normal distribution]] is a probability distribution that is bell-shaped and symmetric about the mean $\mu$.
The graph of a normal distribution is called a [[kw:normal curve]]. The total area under the curve is exactly $1$.
The [[kw:Empirical Rule]] (68‑95‑99.7 rule) states:
• About 68% of the data falls within $\mu \pm 1\sigma$.
• About 95% within $\mu \pm 2\sigma$.
• About 99.7% within $\mu \pm 3\sigma$.
Because the curve is symmetric, half of each area lies on each side of the mean. For example, 34% lies between $\mu$ and $\mu+\sigma$.

notes: The areas outside these intervals are split equally in the two tails.
Use these percentages only if the data is approximately normal.
formulaCard.title: Empirical Rule Summary
formulaCard.formula: $$ P(\mu - k\sigma \le x \le \mu + k\sigma) \approx \text{area for } k=1,2,3 $$

explanation: To find the probability that a normally distributed variable $x$ is in an interval:
1. Convert the boundary x-values to z-scores using $z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.
2. Use the standard normal table to find $P(Z \le z)$ for each boundary.
3. For $P(a \le X \le b) = P(Z \le z_b) - P(Z \le z_a)$. For $P(X \ge a) = 1 - P(Z \le z_a)$.
Real‑world problems often ask for percentages, so multiply the probability by 100.

notes: Always sketch the normal curve and shade the region.
For 'between' probabilities, subtract the smaller table value from the larger.
formulaCard.title: Using Z‑Scores to Find Probabilities
formulaCard.formula: $$ P(X \le x) = P\left(Z \le \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right) $$ $$ P(X \ge x) = 1 - P\left(Z \le \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right) $$

formulaCard.title: Normality Check
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Normal: histogram is bell-shaped, symmetric, mean } \approx \text{ median} $$

explanation: A data set has a [[kw:normal distribution]] if its histogram is bell-shaped and symmetric. In a normal distribution, the mean and median are equal.
A distribution is [[kw:skewed left]] if the left tail is longer; the mean is less than the median.
A distribution is [[kw:skewed right]] if the right tail is longer; the mean is greater than the median.
You cannot use the normal model for skewed distributions – the empirical rule and z‑score methods assume normality.

examples.prompt: Heights of guayule plants are N(12,2). Find the probability a randomly chosen plant is between 7 and 14 inches.
examples.title: Example A – Between Two Values
steps: Understand: μ=12, σ=2. a=7, b=14.
Conclude: About 83.5% of plants have heights between 7 and 14 inches.

examples.title: Example B – At Least a Value
examples.prompt: For the same plants N(12,2), find the probability a plant is at least 16 inches tall.
steps: Understand: We want P(X ≥ 16). 16 is μ + 2σ.
Solve: Using empirical rule, 2σ above mean: tail area = 2.5% (half of 5%). So P ≈ 0.025. With table: z=2, P(Z≤2)=0.9772, P=1-0.9772=0.0228.
Conclude: About 2.3% of plants are at least 16 inches tall.

formulaCard.title: Normal Probability Blueprint

explanation: 1. [[imp:Understand]]: Identify the mean $\mu$, standard deviation $\sigma$, and the interval of interest. Sketch the normal curve and shade the region.
2. [[imp:Solve]]: Convert boundaries to z-scores if needed. Use the standard normal table or the empirical rule to find the probability. For 'at least' or 'more than', use complements.
3. [[imp:Conclude]]: State the probability as a decimal or percent, and interpret it in the context of the problem.
